title: Trade and Domestic Production Networks
text:
← Reading list · Meeting with Yannis
Dhyne, Kikkawa, Mogstad, Tintelnot · 2021 · REStud
Source / paper link
Discussion draft, 20 October 2026. Prepared with reading assistance; to review before the meeting.
Source/version: NBER Working Paper 25120, October 2018, revised January 2019; library record says Dhyne et al. 2021.
Reading scope: Introduction, data/exposure findings, network-formation explanation and concluding counterfactual comparison.

title: Trade and Domestic Production Networks
text:
My short version
A firm can be strongly exposed to foreign inputs even if it never imports directly. It may buy from domestic firms that import, or from their customers. The paper makes this indirect exposure visible with Belgian transaction data. It also shows why letting buyer–supplier links change matters more for large trade shocks than for small ones (PDF pp. 2–5, 41).

title: Trade and Domestic Production Networks
text:
How the paper gets there
Domestic VAT transactions are linked to customs/intra-EU trade records and annual accounts. The authors first study a fixed network and then allow supplier choices with link-specific fixed costs. To keep network formation tractable, eligible suppliers follow an ordering that produces an acyclic network. They estimate the model and compare foreign-price counterfactuals. The large-shock results are model-based exercises, not observed impacts of a particular tariff announcement.

title: Trade and Domestic Production Networks
section: Why I am keeping it for an OM project
text:
Why I am keeping it for an OM project
This is a foundation for questioning “domestic sourcing” as a resilience metric. For an OM project I would ask how a buyer should choose among domestic suppliers with different hidden imported-input content. A feasible first model might use bounds on upstream exposure rather than require complete tier-2 data. The practical decision would be allocation across suppliers, and the performance measure would be expected cost plus shortage risk.

title: Trade and Domestic Production Networks
section: What I still need to be careful about
text:
What I still need to be careful about
VAT and customs microdata are not ordinary public downloads. The acyclic approximation helps computation but is still a modeling restriction. A sourcing change that looks optimal after a shock also may require qualification time absent from a static comparison. I should distinguish an exposure-accounting project from an optimization contribution.

title: Trade and Domestic Production Networks
text:
Questions for Yannis
Could partial information about indirect imports be sufficient for a useful sourcing rule? What access would we realistically have to firm-to-firm transaction data, and what could be done if it is unavailable?

title: The Return to Protectionism
text:
← Reading list · Meeting with Yannis
Fajgelbaum, Goldberg, Kennedy, Khandelwal · 2020 · QJE
Source / paper link
Discussion draft, 20 October 2026. Prepared with reading assistance; to review before the meeting.
Source/version: QJE advance-article PDF, 2019 download, for the article published in 2020.
Reading scope: Introduction, tariff-incidence findings, identification caveats and aggregate/regional interpretation.

title: The Return to Protectionism
text:
My short version
The central result I need is about who pays for tariffs. In the 2018 episode studied here, the authors find essentially complete pass-through into duty-inclusive import prices. That means domestic buyers of imports bear substantial costs; the foreign exporter does not simply absorb the tariff. The small net aggregate estimate also hides much larger transfers and uneven regional effects (PDF pp. 2–5).

title: The Return to Protectionism
text:
How the paper gets there
The authors use product–origin tariff variation to estimate trade-demand and export-supply responses, with event-study and pre-trend checks. They then combine the estimates with a supply-side model for aggregate and regional calculations. In this version, the $51 billion import-buyer loss is a gross component, while the $7.2 billion aggregate real-income loss is net of producer gains and tariff revenue. These are different quantities. The net estimate is not statistically distinguishable from zero at conventional levels once parameter uncertainty is considered.

title: The Return to Protectionism
section: Why I am keeping it for an OM project
text:
Why I am keeping it for an OM project
This motivates a buyer-level problem about tariff uncertainty and inventory. A buyer can front-load orders, wait, qualify an alternative or reserve capacity. I would ask when a temporary buffer dominates costly supplier replacement, given uncertain policy duration and long replenishment lead times. The paper establishes that costs matter; it does not solve that operational decision.

title: The Return to Protectionism
section: What I still need to be careful about
text:
What I still need to be careful about
These are short-run results for the 2018 tariffs, not a universal pass-through parameter for every product in 2026. Country-time and product-time controls also remove some broader price movements. Treating tariffs as instruments requires assumptions; political targeting is a reason to inspect identification carefully.

title: The Return to Protectionism
text:
Questions for Yannis
Can an empirical project connect pre-announcement exposure to inventory and supplier-switching responses? How could we distinguish tariff avoidance from demand changes and routine seasonal ordering?

title: The Macroeconomics of Supply Chain Disruptions
text:
← Reading list · Meeting with Yannis
Acemoglu, Tahbaz-Salehi · 2025 · REStud
Source / paper link
Discussion draft, 20 October 2026. Prepared with reading assistance; to review before the meeting.
Source/version: Published article, Review of Economic Studies 92 (2025), 656–695.
Reading scope: Introduction; model setup and equilibrium distinction; fragility discussion; conclusion. Technical proofs not independently checked.

title: The Macroeconomics of Supply Chain Disruptions
text:
My short version
The useful point for me is that a supply relationship is more than a spot purchase. It takes investment to make an input work for a particular customer, and the relationship creates extra productivity. A shock can make one of these relationships no longer privately worthwhile. When it disappears, other relationships become less attractive too. This can produce a cascade and a sudden output drop even from a small initial change. The sharp result is that this fragility need not be technologically unavoidable: the efficient allocation is continuous in the same shocks. The decentralized incentives to keep links alive are part of the problem (PDF pp. 2–5, 18–25).

title: The Macroeconomics of Supply Chain Disruptions
text:
How the paper gets there
The authors combine a firm-level production network, fixed relationship costs and pairwise Nash bargaining. Two-part tariffs separate marginal input prices from surplus transfers. With a fixed network the equilibrium is efficient; once firms choose links, the network can be too small because a pair does not capture all the benefits it creates elsewhere. I need to keep the uniqueness claims straight: the fixed-network equilibrium is generically unique, while the endogenous network can have multiple equilibria and a greatest equilibrium under the stated complementarity assumptions.

title: The Macroeconomics of Supply Chain Disruptions
section: Why I am keeping it for an OM project
text:
Why I am keeping it for an OM project
An OM version could ask which supplier-support contract keeps a critical relationship alive when a temporary cost shock hits. The decision would be a retention payment, minimum purchase commitment or shared investment, rather than a general recommendation to reshore. I would start with a buyer and two upstream tiers, then compare private profit with network-wide lost production. Qualification time and substitutability would matter a lot.

title: The Macroeconomics of Supply Chain Disruptions
section: What I still need to be careful about
text:
What I still need to be careful about
This is a mechanism paper, not an estimate of the effect of current tariffs. Relationships are selected after shocks in the baseline, so it is not already a model of ex ante safety stock or backup qualification. The supermodularity assumptions limit strong substitution. Adding uncertainty or contracts is an extension the authors themselves mention, so that alone is not a new contribution.

title: The Macroeconomics of Supply Chain Disruptions
text:
Questions for Yannis
Can I formulate a small supplier-retention problem that has a managerial decision and still preserves the externality? What observable evidence would distinguish inefficient link dissolution from an efficient switch to a better supplier?

title: The humble hero: containers have been more important for globalisation than freer trade
text:
← Reading list · Meeting with Yannis
The Economist · 2013 · The Economist
Source / paper link
Discussion draft, 20 October 2026. Prepared with reading assistance; to review before the meeting.
Source/version: The Economist, May 18, 2013; three-page local excerpt.
Reading scope: Complete local three-page excerpt.

title: The humble hero: containers have been more important for globalisation than freer trade
text:
My short version
The helpful idea is that a simple operating standard can change an entire production system. Containers made loading faster and delivery more predictable, which enabled firms to coordinate longer supply chains and leaner inventories. The benefit was not just a cheaper ocean freight rate. That makes this a useful reminder to look for a specific coordination friction instead of assuming that a high-impact OM idea must involve a complicated new algorithm.

title: The humble hero: containers have been more important for globalisation than freer trade
text:
How the paper gets there
The article reports an academic study of container adoption and bilateral trade, including pre-adoption checks. It is journalism discussing another study; the article itself does not provide enough detail for me to evaluate that study's identification. I would read the underlying Bernhofen–El-Sahli–Kneller paper before citing the reported magnitudes as evidence (PDF pp. 1–2).

title: The humble hero: containers have been more important for globalisation than freer trade
section: Why I am keeping it for an OM project
text:
Why I am keeping it for an OM project
A present-day analogue might be input standards, interoperable supplier documentation or reusable qualification records. The decision is whether several buyers should coordinate on a standard despite implementation costs. An interesting trade-off is that standardization can make switching easier while also encouraging everyone to depend on the same infrastructure.

title: The humble hero: containers have been more important for globalisation than freer trade
section: What I still need to be careful about
text:
What I still need to be careful about
I should not repeat the headline that containers matter more than trade agreements as if it were a timeless causal ranking. Historical adoption, infrastructure and policy changed together. This is useful motivation; it does not establish that any modern platform or technology will have a comparable effect.

title: The humble hero: containers have been more important for globalisation than freer trade
text:
Questions for Yannis
Is there a concrete modern coordination bottleneck in an industry we can access? Would the research be about adoption incentives, the value of reduced lead-time uncertainty, or concentration created by a shared standard?

title: Supply Chain Disruptions: Evidence from the Great East Japan Earthquake
text:
← Reading list · Meeting with Yannis
Carvalho, Nirei, Saito, Tahbaz-Salehi · 2021 · QJE
Source / paper link
Discussion draft, 20 October 2026. Prepared with reading assistance; to review before the meeting.
Source/version: Local PDF is a December 2016 working paper; library record points to the 2021 published article.
Reading scope: Introduction, identification logic, reported propagation results and model interpretation. Numbers below belong to the 2016 PDF.

title: Supply Chain Disruptions: Evidence from the Great East Japan Earthquake
text:
My short version
This gives concrete evidence that a local shock reaches firms outside the disaster area through supply links. Both customers and suppliers of earthquake-hit firms suffer, and the effects extend beyond direct partners. The downstream effects are stronger in this version. What matters for my research search is that being geographically far from a disaster is not the same as being economically unexposed (PDF pp. 1–5).

title: Supply Chain Disruptions: Evidence from the Great East Japan Earthquake
text:
How the paper gets there
The study combines Japanese firm-level supplier/customer relationships and firm locations, exploiting the localized 2011 earthquake. It compares subsequent sales growth across different network distances from affected firms, checks pre-event patterns and tests whether electricity shortages explain the findings. In this working-paper version, direct customers underperform controls by 2 percentage points and direct suppliers by 1.2 points. The reported aggregate figure is a 1.2-percentage-point decline in gross output from propagation; that is not a GDP estimate and should not be substituted for the published article's number.

title: Supply Chain Disruptions: Evidence from the Great East Japan Earthquake
section: Why I am keeping it for an OM project
text:
Why I am keeping it for an OM project
A follow-up OM question would ask which pre-event choices shorten recovery: inventory, input standardization, previously qualified backups or a less-overlapping supplier portfolio. I would need to observe these choices before the event. Otherwise faster recovery may simply reflect better firms having both better policies and better outcomes.

title: Supply Chain Disruptions: Evidence from the Great East Japan Earthquake
section: What I still need to be careful about
text:
What I still need to be careful about
The earthquake offers plausibly exogenous shock timing, but firms' network positions and mitigation policies are not randomly assigned. Link data can be incomplete, headquarters are not always production sites, and sales are not a direct stockout measure. A new study needs to handle spillovers to its comparison firms rather than calling all unaffected locations an untreated control group.

title: Supply Chain Disruptions: Evidence from the Great East Japan Earthquake
text:
Questions for Yannis
Could I use an event study around a localized disruption with exposure measured before the event? How would we separate the value of backup qualification from the underlying quality of the buyer?

title: Smart Predict, then Optimize
text:
← Reading list · Meeting with Yannis
Elmachtoub, Grigas · 2022 · Management Science
Source / paper link
Discussion draft, 20 October 2026. Prepared with reading assistance; to review before the meeting.
Source/version: Author manuscript, arXiv 1710.08005v5, November 19, 2020; library record says 2022.
Reading scope: Framework, illustrative routing example, SPO+ construction/consistency statement, experiments and conclusion. Proofs not independently checked.

title: Smart Predict, then Optimize
text:
My short version
A more accurate prediction need not lead to a better decision. If a small error changes which supplier or route I choose, it can matter much more than a large error that leaves the choice unchanged. SPO measures the cost of the induced decision rather than ordinary prediction error. The practical appeal is that the final workflow can still be predict, then optimize; the training objective is what changes (PDF pp. 1–5, 14).

title: Smart Predict, then Optimize
text:
How the paper gets there
The framework predicts coefficients in a linear objective over a known feasible set. Because the true SPO loss is difficult and potentially discontinuous, the authors derive the convex SPO+ surrogate and give consistency results under distributional conditions. Shortest-path and portfolio experiments compare it with least squares, absolute loss and random forests. The reported advantages are strongest under model misspecification; it is not a theorem that SPO+ beats all predictors in all settings (PDF pp. 26–31).

title: Smart Predict, then Optimize
section: Why I am keeping it for an OM project
text:
Why I am keeping it for an OM project
For supply-chain research, I would use this to evaluate whether extra network information changes a sourcing or inventory action. Predicting an upstream link more accurately is only useful if the decision improves. A project could compare an audited extraction pipeline, a simple exposure score and decision-focused learning under missing tier-2 links. The outcome should be cost, fill rate and tail shortage, not just link-prediction accuracy.

title: Smart Predict, then Optimize
section: What I still need to be careful about
text:
What I still need to be careful about

title: Restructuring Global Supply Chains: Navigating Challenges of the COVID-19 Pandemic and Beyond
text:
My short version
This is probably the best starting point for the conversation with Yannis because it connects global restructuring to concrete OM decisions. During 2019–2021 firms added suppliers mostly within existing sourcing locations, shifted volumes away from China and changed shipment patterns. Diversifying suppliers and diversifying countries are therefore separate actions. The paper also makes clear that there is no single response that fits all industries (PDF pp. 6–11).

title: Restructuring Global Supply Chains: Navigating Challenges of the COVID-19 Pandemic and Beyond
text:
How the paper gets there
The study uses Panjiva U.S. sea-import bills of lading merged with Compustat. The final matched sample has 1,533 listed U.S. importers, 4,444 HS6 product codes and 284,017 firm-product-quarter observations; 1,139 firms appear in both periods. It studies sourcing countries, supplier portfolios, industry differences and shipment patterns. Lower shipment frequency with larger quantities is consistent with inventory buffering, but a shipment record does not by itself reveal the firm's exact safety-stock policy.

title: Restructuring Global Supply Chains: Navigating Challenges of the COVID-19 Pandemic and Beyond
section: Why I am keeping it for an OM project
text:
Why I am keeping it for an OM project
The next useful step is to connect the observed restructuring choice to subsequent performance. For example: when does adding suppliers within the same country improve recovery, and when does a shared regional or upstream bottleneck erase the benefit? I would want pre-shock sourcing portfolios, lead times, shipment arrivals and a service or financial outcome. A second promising angle is the time needed to qualify a backup before a disruption.

title: Restructuring Global Supply Chains: Navigating Challenges of the COVID-19 Pandemic and Beyond
section: What I still need to be careful about
text:
What I still need to be careful about
This is observational evidence and a research agenda, not proof that every observed response caused better resilience. Sea shipments miss air/land trade and the sample is not every firm in the economy. The authors explicitly note that lower-tier responses are unobserved. Their proposed research questions mean I cannot claim “study tier-2 visibility” is a novel idea by itself.

title: Restructuring Global Supply Chains: Navigating Challenges of the COVID-19 Pandemic and Beyond
text:
Questions for Yannis
Which of the agenda questions could become a first-year-sized project with a clear decision and accessible data? Could we distinguish supplier diversification that actually reduces correlated risk from diversification that only changes the supplier count?

Source / paper link

Reading scope: Introduction, data construction, simultaneous-equation approach, results and inventory-benchmark implications.

title: Managing Global Sourcing: Inventory Performance
text:
My short version
The clean distinction is inventory units versus dollars tied up in inventory. Overseas sourcing can mean longer lead times and more physical stock, but cheaper units could offset that in dollar terms. In this sample the stock effect dominates: greater global sourcing is associated with higher inventory investment. Supplier diversification can reduce that burden. This gives me an operational channel linking sourcing choices to working capital (PDF pp. 3–5).

title: Managing Global Sourcing: Inventory Performance
text:
How the paper gets there
The authors match U.S. sea-import manifests from 2007–2010 with Compustat for public wholesale/retail firms. They construct sourcing-share and supplier-dispersion measures and jointly model inventory, cost of goods sold and gross margin. In this PDF's estimates, a one-standard-deviation increase in global sourcing corresponds to roughly 22% more inventory investment, and moving from one to two suppliers offsets about 11%. These are sample/model-specific comparisons, not universal causal elasticities.

title: Managing Global Sourcing: Inventory Performance
section: Why I am keeping it for an OM project
text:
Why I am keeping it for an OM project
A current project could ask whether inventory and supplier diversification remain substitutes when suppliers share upstream facilities or ports. With correlated risk, a second name on the supplier list may not reduce the buffer needed. I would model inventory plus sourcing jointly and examine capital tied up, service level and recovery. Financing costs would make the trade-off particularly concrete for smaller firms.

title: Managing Global Sourcing: Inventory Performance
section: What I still need to be careful about
text:
What I still need to be careful about
The sample predates COVID and the recent tariff regime. Inventory is a firm-level accounting quantity, while sourcing data cover sea imports; matching and value estimation introduce measurement issues. Simultaneous equations tackle joint determination only under their identification assumptions. I should not use the 22% number as a forecast for another industry or time period.

title: Managing Global Sourcing: Inventory Performance
text:
Questions for Yannis
Could we obtain shipment and financial data for a replication-style first step? Is the more interesting contribution hidden common exposure, financing constraints, or adjustment dynamics—and which one can we identify cleanly?

Source / paper link

Reading scope: Abstract, introduction, data description and concluding discussion, including limits of direct-trade measures.

title: Global Supply Chains: The Looming Great Reallocation
text:
My short version
My main takeaway is that changing the country on an import shipment does not necessarily remove the original upstream dependence. The paper documents a shift in direct U.S. imports away from China toward places such as Vietnam and Mexico, without concluding that global trade is simply disappearing. It also flags Chinese input supply and investment in those alternative locations. For my research search, the distinction between direct sourcing and underlying exposure is more useful than the label “deglobalization” (PDF pp. 2–6, 34–35).

title: Global Supply Chains: The Looming Great Reallocation
text:
How the paper gets there
This is a broad empirical assessment using product-level trade data, upstreamness measures, greenfield investment announcements, earnings calls and U.S. manufacturing indicators. Much of the recent evidence covers 2017–2022. It connects several indicators; it is not a firm-level randomized test of whether nearshoring improves resilience. The decline from 21.6% to 16.5% is China's share of U.S. goods imports in 2017 versus 2022, not a current 2026 statistic.

title: Global Supply Chains: The Looming Great Reallocation
section: Why I am keeping it for an OM project
text:
Why I am keeping it for an OM project
A more operational question is whether buyers replacing a Chinese tier-1 supplier reduce common upstream exposure or just pay switching costs. The decision could be which alternative supplier to qualify under incomplete knowledge of tier-2 links. Outcomes could include delivery recovery, stockouts and working capital. Aggregate trade data alone would not identify these buyer decisions.

title: Global Supply Chains: The Looming Great Reallocation
section: What I still need to be careful about
text:
What I still need to be careful about
The country-of-shipment, ownership and input-origin questions are different. Imports from Mexico cannot automatically be called Chinese transshipment. Likewise, new assembly abroad is not proof of an independent upstream ecosystem. I would need a defensible exposure measure and distinguish genuine production relocation from routing changes.

title: Global Supply Chains: The Looming Great Reallocation
text:
Questions for Yannis
Is supplier-level data available to test actual risk reduction? The 2025/2026 follow-up by Alfaro and Chor already studies newer reallocation patterns, so what decision-specific contribution would remain for us?

title: Building an alliance to map global supply networks
text:
My short version
The main obstacle is not only optimizing a supply network; it is knowing enough about the network to make a defensible decision. The authors argue for connecting fragmented national firm-level maps into an international map. VAT records, payments and customs data can reveal different parts of the network, but no one source solves the whole problem. Firms often see their own suppliers without seeing several tiers upstream.

title: Building an alliance to map global supply networks
text:
How the paper gets there
This is a policy/research proposal, not a new estimated intervention effect. It reviews recent microdata developments and sketches a mapping blueprint. Administrative VAT data can give broad domestic coverage; trade data connect across borders. Commercial links often favor large public firms and have limited transparency. Reconstructing missing links is a useful possibility, but a predicted link is not an observed transaction (PDF pp. 2–5).

title: Building an alliance to map global supply networks
section: Why I am keeping it for an OM project
text:
Why I am keeping it for an OM project
I would turn the mapping problem into a value-of-information problem. With a small audit budget, which unknown tier-2 relationships should a buyer verify first before choosing suppliers or reserve capacity? The goal would be better decisions with partial information, rather than building a perfect global map. This could pair well with SPO, but the uncertainty in link existence must remain explicit.

title: Building an alliance to map global supply networks
section: What I still need to be careful about
text:
What I still need to be careful about
Getting access to VAT or bank records is a major institutional hurdle. A supply link does not reveal quantities, substitutability, inventories or unused capacity. Also, missing links are unlikely to be random. A method that works only when links are hidden uniformly at random might look good in a benchmark and fail on smaller or overseas suppliers.

title: Building an alliance to map global supply networks
text:
Questions for Yannis
Can we study targeted supplier verification using a modest, auditable network dataset? What evidence would show that the selected information improves resilience decisions rather than just improving a reconstruction score?

text:

Literature check and discussion draft — 20 October 2026. Prepared with reading assistance; to review with Yannis. This is a targeted search and comparison, not a systematic review or a claim that a gap has been proved.

title: Candidate 1: shared upstream risk
text:
My revised assessment
The starting question is important, but the basic mechanism is already established. Different direct suppliers can share an upstream source; this can change optimal mitigation and transmit financial risk. Neither this observation, adding inventory to it, nor asking whether information has value is sufficient novelty.
My more defensible question to investigate is:

When does verifying a hidden common upstream dependency create usable diversification, once a buyer must qualify and activate an alternative before its inventory buffer is exhausted?

“Usable” is a working description, not a new construct that I can claim to have invented. I mean a product-specific alternative with verified relevant upstream exposure, acceptable quality, available capacity and a feasible activation date. A firm name, different country or predicted link alone does not establish that.
The potential contribution would be a new, well-measured operational fact and a decision mechanism, supported by a convincing comparison with existing models. Its novelty is still conditional. Full-text comparison with the closest information papers is unfinished because several manuscripts could not be accessed.

title: Candidate 1: shared upstream risk
text:
The closest obstacles to novelty
Ang et al. is the first benchmark. Its model already makes a common tier-2 source affect the buyer’s mitigation strategy and suppliers’ incentives. The precise baseline information assumption appears on printed p. 2401 (PDF p. 6). I cannot describe the basic diamond structure or a stock/sourcing comparison as my contribution.
The information question is also crowded. Bakshi–Mohan and its 2025 companion directly challenge the idea that “we add an audit” is enough. The latter’s abstract even reports a non-obvious comparative static for perfect-information value. I must obtain both full texts before making a theorem-level novelty claim.
Measurement and action are established concerns too. Culot warns about interpreting corporate relationships as relevant product flows, Mungo discusses substantive evaluation, and the September 2026 JBL paper addresses conversion of visibility into action. The remaining opportunity needs a specific decision, observable constraint and result beyond those general messages.

title: Candidate 1: shared upstream risk
section: The candidate contribution I would test first
text:
The candidate contribution I would test first
A working title is “From supplier diversification to a ready alternative: the operating value of verifying shared upstream dependence.” This is a project description, not a submission-ready title.
I would narrow to one input family and one critical process stage. The initial decision maker is one buyer. Before a disruption, it can spend a limited budget on verifying a suspected common dependency, qualifying an independently exposed alternative, or holding a buffer. Qualification takes time; a claimed alternate supplier may lack the required grade, process approval or reserved capacity.
The proposed mechanism is that information and readiness can be complements. Learning the correct bottleneck may be valuable only when it changes a feasible action in time. Conversely, qualification can be wasted if the nominal alternative relies on the same constrained source. These are hypotheses to test against the literature, not results established by this review.
A small example helps state the distinction. If inventory covers 20 days but a genuinely independent alternative needs 60 days for approval, discovering that alternative during the disruption does not protect the first uncovered weeks. An already qualified source may help, but only if it has accessible capacity and does not share the affected bottleneck. These numbers are hypothetical. This example is not a novel theorem; recovery/coverage logic has substantial prior work.
What would make the project more than an incremental model? At least one of the following, with evidence:

A documented decision reversal: the same budget produces a different preferred action once product/site dependence and qualification feasibility replace a supplier-name count. Show when an established, correctly implemented baseline would not already recommend that action.
A credible estimate of the benefit of information conditional on operational readiness, using observed procurement and service outcomes rather than risk perceptions alone.
A quantitatively important, validated mismeasurement result: nominal diversification systematically misstates relevant independence in the selected setting, and correcting it materially changes a real decision. This needs more than showing that some database links are wrong.

I would begin with the second route if we have a partner and decision logs. Otherwise, I would start with a small model and an openly reproducible sector pilot, while being explicit that the pilot does not establish firm-level performance or publication-level novelty.

title: Candidate 1: shared upstream risk
section: Evidence and data I would need
text:
Evidence and data I would need
The useful unit is buyer–part or material grade–production site–date, not just buyer–supplier firm. Minimum fields are:

Direct source and the specific common upstream process/site, with evidence and verification date.
Whether an alternative is technically qualified for the same requirement; qualification start/end dates and any approval restrictions.
Available or reserved capacity, lead time, inventory coverage and the actual contingency chosen.
Disruption timing and operating outcomes: unfilled units, delivery delay, downtime, expediting cost and recovery.

Keep four distinctions separate: unobserved is not independent; common ownership is not necessarily a common physical bottleneck; a shared node is not necessarily relevant to the focal product; and a technically feasible alternative is not necessarily available under widespread stress.
A sample of 10–30 verified part/site cases could expose measurement and access problems before a larger project. That would be a feasibility exercise, not a sufficient sample for a general causal conclusion. A suitable power calculation and dependence structure would be needed for an evaluation design.

A feasible public-data starting point
Cheng et al. provide public code and data and an archived release. The repository has processed flows, raw trade files and analysis scripts. It offers a concrete way to reproduce stage-level dependence and uncertainty bounds. The material is historical and aggregated by country, and some inputs are embedded in scripts. I have verified availability, not run a replication.
The June 2025 correction changes two labels in Fig. 4e and adds a rounding note; it is attached with the corrected paper. A pilot must use the corrected version. Public flows cannot substitute for product qualification or actual reserved-capacity data.
Panjiva or FactSet could provide signals and a sampling frame if our institution has access. Neither should be treated as a complete bill of materials. A missing edge is not proof that two alternatives are independent. The Brazilian transactions used by Monteiro et al. are proprietary; their existence is not evidence that our group can obtain them.

section: How to distinguish an OM contribution from an algorithm project
text:
How to distinguish an OM contribution from an algorithm project
The central outcome is an operating decision and its consequences: which verification, buffer or qualification investment should a buyer make, and what service or cost improves? A new optimizer, larger graph or more accurate link classifier would be a tool, not the core claim.
A first model could hold demand and other buyers’ behavior simple and compare:

The buyer’s current rule and a nominal supplier-count rule.
Known correlated risk with a correctly implemented Ang-style incentive/sourcing benchmark.
A Ford-style exposure/contingency baseline once its full model is reviewed.
Fixed versus targeted verification; qualification-only and buffer-only policies.
A full-information benchmark with the same physical capacity and timing constraints.

Do not handicap the baselines by pretending that the literature assumes independent suppliers when it does not. Report total cost, service, severe shortfall and realized recovery, including verification and qualification costs. Evaluate map errors that disproportionately hide critical links, not only random deletion.
If budget accounting treats audit spending and inventory spending as substitutes, that is a modeling choice to justify, not an empirical fact. The first result should remain visible in a small example; complexity can come later.

title: Candidate 1: shared upstream risk
section: A credible empirical route, if data exist
text:
A credible empirical route, if data exist
A partner’s phased introduction of verified upstream information could provide a setting, but voluntary adoption is endogenous: better firms may map more, and disrupted firms may map after a problem. Information-arrival timestamps are also often influenced by anticipated risk.
A field design could compare normal planning, verified dependency information, and information plus a defined prequalification support process. Randomization would need to respect shared suppliers and spillovers; withholding already-known safety-critical information would not be an appropriate design. The implementation and sample requirements would have to be agreed with a partner. There is no experiment in place.
Without randomization, a phased rollout or other external variation might support identification only after examining assignment, anticipation, pretrends, demand shifts and concurrent changes. A simple event study does not solve those problems. A descriptive paper should label its estimates as descriptive.
The high-value outcome would connect what was learned → what action became feasible → what was actually changed → what operating consequence followed. Interview explanations can guide the mechanism but cannot replace performance evidence.

title: Candidate 1: shared upstream risk
text:
Why the broader journals matter
I would borrow the question selection and breadth of these outlets, not assume that a small sourcing model fits all of them.

Science: Pichler et al. (2023), already in the library, motivates network visibility as a broad data and coordination problem. Our narrower contribution must identify the buyer action enabled by better information.
Nature Communications: Cheng et al. gives a concrete, societally important battery setting. It is not the flagship Nature. A strong sector study would need physical/process knowledge and defensible data, not only a general supplier graph.
Nature: Guan’s October 2026 piece is a Comment. It motivates common infrastructure dependencies but is not causal evidence. Digital/energy dependencies are a later application unless we can observe and act on one of them clearly.
Econometrica: Kopytov et al. (2024), already in the library, reminds me that safer sourcing and efficient resource allocation are different questions. Lower volatility is not automatically welfare improvement.
QJE: Grossman–Helpman–Sabal distinguishes private protective investment from network-wide incentives. A subsidy or public information-sharing proposal would require an explicit externality, not just a buyer saving money.
The Economist: Useful for finding contemporary cases and explaining why someone should care. It does not establish a literature gap or identify a causal effect. I did not add a tangential or inaccessible article merely to include the outlet.

A buyer-level operating result could naturally be assessed in OM outlets such as Management Science, MSOM, POM or JOM, depending on method and evidence. A claim about society-wide resilience would need broader validation. No venue or acceptance probability is implied by this review.

title: Candidate 1: shared upstream risk
section: What I would say to Yannis
text:
What I would say to Yannis

“The closer search changed my view. The common tier-2 problem is already modeled by Ang and coauthors and studied empirically by Wang and coauthors. There are also direct papers on network information and its value. So I would not pitch hidden dependence itself as new. I would like to investigate when learning a product-specific dependency changes a feasible mitigation action, especially when qualifying an independent alternative takes longer than the inventory buffer. I think the first task is to establish whether we can observe that decision and whether it remains distinct from those benchmarks.”


Questions he may ask







Question
My answer at this stage




“What exactly is new?”
Not yet established. The candidate margin is verified information interacting with readiness for a specific product and bottleneck, with operating outcomes. I must compare the closest full texts first.


“Isn’t this Ang plus an information cost?”
It would be too incremental if that is all it becomes. I need a mechanism or empirical decision effect not already implied by its known-configuration model and existing information-value work.


“Isn’t this just time-to-recover versus inventory coverage?”
Timing itself is established. The proposed test is how product-specific learning changes which independent response can be qualified in time, evaluated against exposure/contingency baselines.


“Why not map everything?”
Full mapping is costly and may not change feasible actions; that general insight already has prior work. We would need to show a specific allocation of verification and readiness effort that changes an important decision.


“Where is the data?”
Open battery flows permit a limited pilot. The actual buyer question requires product/site, qualification, capacity and outcome data; we have not confirmed access.


“What if independence cannot be observed?”
Then we cannot certify it from missing commercial links. We should narrow to a validated subnetwork or change the question.


“Is this general interest?”
The broad problem is whether costly de-risking buys continuity. The contribution would need a compelling fact and a clear operating mechanism. Journal labels cannot supply either.


“Why not model all firms and policy?”
That would add a second project. First establish the buyer decision; only then ask whether its incentives differ from network welfare.

title: Candidate 1: shared upstream risk
section: First milestones and reasons to stop
text:
First milestones and reasons to stop

Read Ang’s model alongside the full Wang article, Bakshi–Mohan, Bakshi’s companion, the latest Osadchiy manuscript and the Ford implementation. The inaccessible texts are a genuine remaining comparison task.
Write a one-page assumption comparison: known versus uncertain topology; static versus changing links; perfect versus noisy signals; stock position; qualification; actual capacity; decentralized incentives; operating versus financial outcomes. Do not infer absent assumptions from abstracts.
Check whether a firm partner or an existing institutional dataset can supply the minimum fields. Select one input family only after this check.
Reproduce a public-data baseline and a small decision example. Predefine what would count as a meaningful action change.
Stop or pivot if a closest paper already solves the same choice, independence cannot be validated, the decision improvement disappears against a fair baseline, or feasible data cannot measure the operating outcome.

title: Meeting with Yannis
section: What I want to get out of the meeting
text:
What I want to get out of the meeting
I want to move from “supply-chain resilience is important” to a small question where a manager makes a specific decision and the answer could change that decision. The reading suggests that supplier count, country count and purchase price can each miss something important. My strongest initial interest is in the difference between apparent diversification and actual independence.
These are research candidates, not verified literature gaps. I have reviewed selected substantive sections of the local papers for mechanisms, evidence and limitations; I have not independently checked every proof or replicated the estimates. The book note is based on selected passages. Tomlin is an abstract-only note because the full text was unavailable. The Chinese-firms note uses the accessible Economist publication on Mint, not the paid Substack continuation.

title: Meeting with Yannis
section: Three distinctions I should be able to explain
text:
Three distinctions I should be able to explain

Supplier diversity versus risk diversity. Several suppliers can share one upstream input, region or transport route. Adding a supplier need not add independent capacity. Niu et al. distinguish supplier and geographic diversification; Dhyne et al. and Baldwin–Freeman explain indirect exposure.
Output stability versus welfare or profit. Kopytov et al. show a potentially efficient cost of flight to safety. Acemoglu–Tahbaz-Salehi and Elliott et al. show different mechanisms that can make decentralized networks inefficiently fragile. These are different models, not contradictory empirical estimates.
A prediction versus a decision. Pichler et al. motivate learning about upstream links. SPO explains why prediction accuracy alone is not the operating objective. More accurate mapping is useful only if the buyer makes a better action, with feasibility checked separately.

title: Meeting with Yannis
section: 1. My first candidate: when does a second supplier actually protect me?
text:
1. My first candidate: when does a second supplier actually protect me?
Question. How should a buyer choose inventory and reserve backup capacity when two apparently different suppliers may share a critical upstream bottleneck, and verifying that dependence is costly?
Why it might matter. A firm could pay qualification costs and still discover during a disruption that both sources fail together. Conversely, always demanding completely independent chains could be unnecessarily expensive. The useful answer would tell the buyer when to investigate, when to hold stock, and when to pay for an independent source.
A small starting model. One buyer, one product, two regular sources and one expensive outside option. Before the shock, choose an audit, buffer stock and reserved capacity under a common budget. An audit updates the probability of shared upstream exposure; it is not assumed to reveal the whole network perfectly. After the shock, allocate the capacity actually available. Demand can initially be simple so that the information and supply mechanisms are visible.
The result I would look for. Conditions under which a third nominal source adds less value than verifying an existing source or protecting the common bottleneck. The comparison would report expected total cost, fill rate, severe-shortage probability and the value of the audit. I would compare with no-audit dual sourcing, inventory-only protection, a conservative policy and a full-information benchmark.
Data and credibility. First reproduce a small analytical/numerical example. For validation, seek a partner with a known bill of materials and a few verified upstream links. Commercial shipment links or disclosures could provide additional signals, but should not be treated as the complete network. Test nonrandom missing links and false positives. Synthetic results would demonstrate a mechanism, not establish real-world savings.
Novelty risk. Correlated failures, multitier risk, capacity reservation and information acquisition all have substantial prior literatures. Combining them is not automatically a contribution. I need to identify the closest models and show a decision reversal or a measurable value-of-information result that they do not already imply. Start centrally; competing buyers sharing the backup is a possible later extension, not an extra feature to add immediately.

title: Meeting with Yannis
section: 2. A more empirical candidate: buffer now or change supplier?
text:
2. A more empirical candidate: buffer now or change supplier?
Question. When a policy shock has uncertain duration, when should an importer front-load inventory, qualify a replacement or wait?
Decision and mechanism. Sourcing changes have sunk costs and qualification delays; inventory is quicker but ties up capital and can become obsolete. The belief that a policy will last can therefore matter as much as the current tariff. Separate announcement, implementation and realized delivery delays. Do not assume a policy coefficient from 2018 applies unchanged today.
Possible design. Use pre-event product/country exposure and a well-defined policy episode. Measure supplier entry/exit, shipment timing, inventory dollars and recovery, with event-study diagnostics. Anticipation, seasonal orders, demand changes and indirect exposure of comparison firms threaten identification. Policy assignment is not random; an event study is not by itself a causal design. A smaller descriptive replication may be the appropriate first step.
Feasibility. Panjiva-style shipment data and Compustat access would help, but must be checked before selecting the project. Public aggregate trade data can support a pilot on patterns, not identify a buyer's inventory or qualification policy. I would narrow to one industry where substitution and product perishability can be characterized.
Novelty risk. Recent Alfaro–Chor work already studies delayed reallocation in sticky and contract-intensive goods. My contribution would need to be the operational inventory/qualification trade-off or credible firm-level performance evidence, not another graph of imports shifting away from China.

title: Meeting with Yannis
section: 3. A methods candidate: which supplier information is worth paying for?
text:
3. A methods candidate: which supplier information is worth paying for?
Question. With a limited verification budget, which uncertain supplier relationships should be checked to improve an actual sourcing decision?
Approach. Start with a small sourcing problem and compare spend-based auditing, network-centrality auditing, uncertainty sampling and decision-based auditing. Include audit cost, incorrect extracted links and hard feasibility checks. If text or an LLM is used to propose links, keep the source evidence and require verification before treating capacity as real. A fluent supplier explanation is not a capacity certificate.
Contribution test. The method should improve total operating cost or shortage risk on held-out decisions, not only link-prediction accuracy. Test rare disruptions, changes in correlations and geographic shifts. The original SPO paper assumes unknown objective coefficients and a known feasible set; I cannot simply inherit its guarantees for uncertain network feasibility.
Feasibility and priority. This is attractive if we have auditable network data and methods supervision. Without those, it risks becoming a generic “AI for supply chains” project. I would use it as a precise version of candidate 1 rather than try to build a general supply-chain agent.

title: Meeting with Yannis
section: Recent literature check — what already overlaps
text:
Recent literature check — what already overlaps
Targeted check through 20 October 2026, not a systematic literature review. The sources below were checked at publisher abstracts or overview level; none is represented as an additional fully reviewed paper.

Alfaro & Chor, An Anatomy of the Great Reallocation in US Supply Chain Trade, NBER 34490 — issued November 2025, revised April 2026. Its abstract describes newer U.S. sourcing shifts and the later adjustment of relationship-sticky goods. This is the immediate follow-up to the 2023 reading, so “firms reallocate slowly” is not enough for novelty.
Chen & Shi, Tailored Base-Surge Policies in Dual-Sourcing Inventory Systems with Demand Learning — online December 2024, Operations Research 73(4), 2025. It learns a dual-sourcing inventory policy from censored demand and gives regret guarantees relative to the best TBS policy. Learning demand with two sources is already a developed problem.
Chen, Chou & Sun, Process Flexibility: A Distribution-Free Approach to Long Chain Resilience — online August 2025, Operations Research 74(1), 2026. It provides distribution-free performance bounds for flexible capacity networks under disruptions. “Flexibility helps under uncertain distributions” is not an open result by itself. This paper's process-flexibility long chain should not be confused with long international shipping chains.
Cohen, Dai, Perakis et al., Supply Chain Management in the AI Era: A Vision Statement from the Operations Management Community — MSOM, online March 26, 2026. It emphasizes integrating learning with OM structure, reliable data and human decision making. It is an agenda/vision article, not causal evidence that an AI system improves resilience.

title: Meeting with Yannis
text:
Small glossary for the meeting

Extensive margin: adding or removing a supplier link. Intensive margin: changing purchases through an existing link.
Domar weight: a producer's sales divided by aggregate value added/GDP; it reflects economic importance in these models and is not simply its profit share.
Externality: my action changes someone else's outcome in a way I do not fully count in my private decision.
Calibration: choosing model parameters to match selected data features. A counterfactual from that model is not automatically a causal estimate.
Regret: the performance gap from a specified information-rich benchmark. The benchmark must be named; it is not necessarily the unconstrained optimal policy.
Fill rate versus tail shortage: the average fraction of demand served can look good while a few scenarios still have very severe losses. I should measure both when the question is resilience.

My short version
This is much closer to my first idea than I initially realized. Two tier-1 suppliers can share a risky tier-2 source. title: Endogenous Production Networks Under Supply Chain Uncertainty
text:
My short version
I read this as a warning against measuring resilience only by output volatility. Firms can move toward safer suppliers, reducing volatility but also giving up productivity. In this model that can be an efficient trade-off, rather than a failure to maximize GDP. The timing is important: firms choose a production technique before productivity shocks are known. Their decisions then reshape both the weights and the links in the network (PDF pp. 1–3). This gives a different explanation for network change from the bargaining externality in Acemoglu and Tahbaz-Salehi.

title: Endogenous Production Networks Under Supply Chain Uncertainty
text:
How the paper gets there
The model has competitive firms, a risk-averse representative household and technique choices that change input shares. It characterizes an efficient equilibrium. A basic U.S. calibration uses 37 BEA sectors, 1948–2020. Additional firm-level evidence uses Compustat/stock volatility and FactSet links: riskier suppliers are more likely to lose relationships. The IV exercises address endogeneity but depend on the instruments' exclusion restrictions. Stock volatility is a proxy for uncertainty, not a direct measure of delivery failure (PDF pp. 31–36).

title: Endogenous Production Networks Under Supply Chain Uncertainty
section: Why I am keeping it for an OM project
text:
Why I am keeping it for an OM project
For a firm-level OM question, I would separate expected cost, disruption risk and the time needed to qualify a replacement. How much should a buyer pay for stability when switching takes months and risk estimates are noisy? An interesting outcome is the cost of stability, not just whether a firm diversifies. I could compare a static safe-supplier choice with a dynamic policy that learns and keeps a backup option.

title: Endogenous Production Networks Under Supply Chain Uncertainty
section: What I still need to be careful about
text:
What I still need to be careful about
The calibration is deliberately stylized and explains only part of network variation. One-year technique adjustment and Cobb–Douglas structure are strong restrictions. I should not read a fall in expected GDP as a fall in welfare. Nor should I assume that the model's efficient flight to safety describes every real supply chain (PDF pp. 32–34).

title: Endogenous Production Networks Under Supply Chain Uncertainty

title: Global supply-chain effects of COVID-19 control measures
text:
My short version
What I take from this is the importance of duration and coordination. A local recovery does not necessarily restore output if connected locations are still constrained. Under the paper's scenarios, longer restrictions can produce substantial indirect losses as shortages work through supply chains. The practical point for me is to distinguish the size of an initial hit from the path of recovery, rather than summarize a disruption with one failure probability.

title: Global supply-chain effects of COVID-19 control measures
text:
How the paper gets there
The authors use an enhanced adaptive regional input–output model with weekly time steps, labor and transport constraints, input substitution and inventory dynamics. They compare 39 idealized combinations of geographic spread, duration, strictness and recovery. The very large percentage losses in the figures are outputs of these scenarios, not observed pandemic GDP estimates or forecasts verified after the fact (PDF pp. 1–3, 6–8).

title: Global supply-chain effects of COVID-19 control measures
section: Why I am keeping it for an OM project
text:
Why I am keeping it for an OM project
An OM version could choose inventory positioning and recovery capacity when a shortage can reappear. Instead of estimating an abstract “pandemic effect”, I would use the logic for a specified hazard, such as several facilities relying on one disrupted corridor. The decision could be how much buffer to hold at each tier and when to activate an alternative route.

title: Global supply-chain effects of COVID-19 control measures
section: What I still need to be careful about
text:
What I still need to be careful about
These are early-pandemic stylized scenarios with strong assumptions about constraints and recovery. The model is not a full epidemiological policy optimization, and I should not turn its lockdown comparison into present-day health advice. Industry-level input–output data also hide firm-level heterogeneity and actual spare capacity.

title: Global supply-chain effects of COVID-19 control measures
text:
Questions for Yannis
Can we model recovery duration and repeated disruption without taking on a whole global economy? What would change in an inventory policy if a quick reopening or recovery is likely to be followed by another interruption?

The model compares a cheaper unreliable source with a more expensive reliable source. Inventory, reliable sourcing and contingent switching serve different purposes. The key distinction is disruption duration: the same average availability can conceal frequent short outages or rare long ones. Longer outages can favor reliable sourcing over inventory. Capacity limits, risk aversion and the backup supplier’s ability to increase volume change which combinations are attractive. I would choose inventory and a reservation quantity before the shock, then allocate emergency capacity afterward. That question is a proposed direction, not a gap established by this abstract.

Source / paper link

Reading scope: Targeted reading of the introduction and selected passages in chapters 14, 19 and 20. This is not a cover-to-cover book summary.

title: Outside the Box: How Globalization Changed from Moving Stuff to Spreading Ideas
text:
My short version
I am using this book for historical context and examples. Its useful reminder is that globalization changes form; cross-border value creation is not the same thing as shipping ever more finished goods. Better transport, communication and coordination made long value chains possible, but firms sometimes treated the purchase-price saving as if it were the full economic saving. The risk examples show why that can be misleading (introduction; chapter 14).

title: Outside the Box: How Globalization Changed from Moving Stuff to Spreading Ideas
text:
How the paper gets there
This is historical narrative drawing on cases, interviews, archival work and published research, rather than a single identification strategy. Chapter 14 follows how cost-focused outsourcing can hide dependence several tiers away. The BMW coating example and the Riken piston-ring disruption make the low-cost-but-critical-input problem concrete. It also describes investments in flexible production, alternative routes and inventory buffers after disruptions (PDF pp. 159–167).

title: Outside the Box: How Globalization Changed from Moving Stuff to Spreading Ideas
section: Why I am keeping it for an OM project
text:
Why I am keeping it for an OM project
The useful OM question is about total cost and the boundary of the firm: when should a buyer standardize an input, keep an outside supplier, qualify another source or retain internal capability? A second question is whether purchasing incentives reward cheap units while ignoring downtime and working capital. These examples help motivate a model; they do not establish its parameters.

title: Outside the Box: How Globalization Changed from Moving Stuff to Spreading Ideas
section: What I still need to be careful about
text:
What I still need to be careful about
I should not present an illustrative case as causal evidence, or the author's historical periodization as a consensus forecast for 2026. I have not reviewed all 287 pages or checked the underlying historical sources. For a meeting, I would use one or two concrete examples and then connect them to formal or empirical papers.

text:

Would an organizational-incentives angle be interesting: purchasing managers optimize price while production bears disruption costs? Can I make this precise enough to generate a testable prediction, rather than simply listing hidden costs?

Source / paper link

Reading scope: Risk taxonomy, exposure/policy discussion and future-research sections; selected review sections.

title: Risks and Global Supply Chains: What We Know and What We Need to Know
text:
My short version
I am keeping this as a map of the problem rather than one new causal result. It asks whether global supply chains are too risky, not merely whether they contain risk. That forces a comparison of risk with the gains from specialization and trade. It also separates shocks that hit supply chains from the propagation caused by supply-chain links. Making a chain domestic may remove one exposure while concentrating it on another (PDF pp. 2–5, 25–27).

title: Risks and Global Supply Chains: What We Know and What We Need to Know
text:
How the paper gets there
The authors review economics and business research and suggest a portfolio-style risk–reward framework. They discuss why direct import dependence misses indirect exposure and why a policy case requires a wedge between private incentives and social costs. Stress testing and better information are useful directions, but neither is a complete operational policy on its own.

title: Risks and Global Supply Chains: What We Know and What We Need to Know
section: Why I am keeping it for an OM project
text:
Why I am keeping it for an OM project
This helps me define a cleaner research objective. Instead of asking “How can we make supply chains resilient?”, I could ask which mix of inventory, qualification and capacity reservation gives the largest service improvement for a given budget under a particular common shock. I would report cost and service outcomes together, and compare with a realistic current policy.

title: Risks and Global Supply Chains: What We Know and What We Need to Know
section: What I still need to be careful about
text:
What I still need to be careful about
It is a review written around the early pandemic period. Statements about what is unknown then need updating before I use them to claim novelty in 2026. It also does not establish that more geographic spread is always beneficial. Risk correlations, substitutability and adaptation costs must be specified.

title: Risks and Global Supply Chains: What We Know and What We Need to Know

Reading scope: Introduction; single-critical-input model; first-best/second-best policy distinction; concluding discussion. Proofs not independently checked.

title: Supply Chain Resilience: Should Policy Promote International Diversification or Reshoring?
text:
My short version
I should not assume that firms always invest too little in resilience. A firm fails to capture all the consumer benefit of keeping its product available, which pushes toward too little investment. But it also wants to be operating when competitors fail, so it can take their business. That can push the other way. Which force dominates depends on demand and the policy instruments available. The paper therefore does not give a blanket argument for subsidizing domestic sourcing (PDF pp. 3–5, 30–31).

title: Supply Chain Resilience: Should Policy Promote International Diversification or Reshoring?
text:
How the paper gets there
Each firm needs one customized critical input and chooses a home supplier, a foreign supplier, both, or exit. Home is safer and more expensive. There are relationship-specific failures and country-level disruptions. The authors compare firms' choices with a planner's choices under differentiated-product competition. With CES preferences, a diversification subsidy achieves the constrained optimum when consumption subsidies are unavailable. With more flexible demand, even the direction of the diversification intervention can change.

title: Supply Chain Resilience: Should Policy Promote International Diversification or Reshoring?
section: Why I am keeping it for an OM project
text:
Why I am keeping it for an OM project
For OM, the promising step is to introduce an operational constraint that makes a policy recommendation different: backup capacity, lead time or inventory. For example, a subsidy for qualifying another supplier might do little if all buyers rely on the same scarce backup. I would want to compare a qualification subsidy with a capacity-reservation subsidy and count both service losses and the fiscal cost.

title: Supply Chain Resilience: Should Policy Promote International Diversification or Reshoring?
section: What I still need to be careful about
text:
What I still need to be careful about
The source itself proposes dynamics, inventories and richer chains as extensions. Those are starting points for a literature search, not evidence of an unfilled gap. The baseline is very simple: one critical input and two countries. Its public-welfare result is different from the privately optimal sourcing policy of a single buyer.

title: Supply Chain Resilience: Should Policy Promote International Diversification or Reshoring?
text:
Questions for Yannis
Could we get a useful result by letting competing buyers reserve the same backup supplier? Would that need a game-theory model, or should I first solve a centralized allocation benchmark?

text:
← Reading list · Meeting with Yannis
Elliott, Golub, Leduc · 2022 · AER
Source / paper link
Discussion draft, 20 October 2026. Prepared with reading assistance; to review before the meeting.
Source/version: Author working-paper PDF, January 7, 2022, arXiv 2001.03853v5; library record says 2022.
Reading scope: Introduction and network setup; main fragility regimes and interpretations. Technical appendices not independently checked.

title: Supply Network Formation and Fragility
text:
My short version
A network can handle isolated supplier failures quite well and still be very vulnerable to a small deterioration affecting many links. That is the distinction I want to remember. Each producer needs several essential input types and has alternative suppliers within each type. For deep, complex production, reliability can change very sharply at a threshold. Firms may end up near that threshold when they choose relationship investment for their own profits, even though a planner would avoid it (PDF pp. 2–6).

title: Supply Network Formation and Fragility
text:
How the paper gets there
This is an analytical network/percolation model. Relationship strength is the probability that a link works, and firms invest to improve it. A firm functions only if it has a working supplier for every essential input, whose own inputs must also work. The authors study reliability first with exogenous strengths and then with strategic investment. They identify productive, fragile and unproductive regimes; the fragile regime occurs over a range of parameters, not just at a single accidental parameter value.

title: Supply Network Formation and Fragility
section: Why I am keeping it for an OM project
text:
Why I am keeping it for an OM project
For OM, the question becomes where to spend a limited reliability budget. I would compare adding another nominal supplier with improving the weakest upstream input category. A useful model could have a finite bill of materials, qualification costs and correlated hazards. The test would be whether policies based on direct supplier reliability miss a large tail-loss exposure.

title: Supply Network Formation and Fragility
section: What I still need to be careful about
text:
What I still need to be careful about
The sharp phase transition depends on the large/deep-network setting. I should not claim that a small finite factory network has a literal discontinuity of the same kind. Multisourcing within an input type and needing multiple input types play different roles. The result is a mechanism, not an estimate of how close today's economy is to a collapse threshold.

title: Supply Network Formation and Fragility
text:
Questions for Yannis
How much of the threshold intuition survives in a finite, heterogeneous supply network? Could an implementable audit or investment rule outperform simple “protect the largest supplier” rankings?

Source / paper link
Discussion draft, 20 October 2026. Prepared with reading assistance; to review before the meeting.
Source/version: Published Econometrica article, September 2012, 1977–2016.
Reading scope: Introduction/network examples, central mechanism and concluding quantitative illustration. Proofs not independently checked.

title: The Network Origins of Aggregate Fluctuations
text:
My short version
The idea I want to retain is that independent small shocks do not necessarily wash out when production is connected asymmetrically. A supplier can matter far beyond its own size because other firms rely on it directly and indirectly. The contrast between a balanced network and a star-shaped network makes this clear. Merely counting links or saying a network is sparse is not enough to infer aggregate risk (PDF pp. 2–5).

title: The Network Origins of Aggregate Fluctuations
text:
How the paper gets there
The authors build a multisector input–output model and study how aggregate volatility changes as the economy is disaggregated. The structure of influence through direct and higher-order supplier connections determines whether the usual diversification argument applies. U.S. input–output data provide an illustrative quantitative exercise, but the paper explicitly says this is not a substitute for a systematic econometric investigation (PDF p. 28).

title: The Network Origins of Aggregate Fluctuations
section: Why I am keeping it for an OM project
text:
Why I am keeping it for an OM project
For OM, this suggests evaluating a supplier-support or audit budget using downstream impact rather than purchase spend alone. A low-spend component producer might be hard to replace and affect many product lines. I would compare spend-based ranking, network-centrality ranking and a decision-based ranking that includes substitution and recovery time.

title: The Network Origins of Aggregate Fluctuations
section: What I still need to be careful about
text:
What I still need to be careful about
This baseline has a fixed production network. It does not establish how an individual firm should adapt its suppliers during a shock. An economically influential node is not automatically the best intervention target: intervention effectiveness and costs can change the ranking. I should also avoid translating an aggregate asymptotic result directly into a finite supplier portfolio.

title: The Network Origins of Aggregate Fluctuations
text:
Questions for Yannis
What would make a supplier-prioritization rule operationally meaningful rather than just another centrality measure? Can we identify cases where a small, replaceable hub matters less than a small, irreplaceable component source?
